text: See that red dot? That's a game. Ninety-six percent of the people who played it liked it.
It came out in 2015, it costs ten bucks, and it has three hundred and two reviews.
And it launched on the exact same day as one of the biggest games of that year.
So I scored fifty-one thousand, eight hundred and ninety-seven games on Steam to answer one question.
Given how good a game is, how many people should have played it? And which games got robbed the hardest?
Here's every one of them. Left to right is how much players liked it. Bottom to top is how many reviews it has.
I'm using reviews as the stand-in for players, because Steam doesn't publish sales.
Better games get more reviews. You'd hope so. That gold line is my model.
You give it a game's rating and the year it came out, and it tells you how many reviews a game like that usually gets.
Quick reality check before anyone yells at me. A review isn't a sale.
For the games on this list, SteamSpy's owner estimates work out to about one review for every hundred people who own it. Bundles do that.
So I'm not saying nobody played these. I'm saying far fewer people cared enough to show up than a game this good normally gets.
A few rules. Only games released from 2014 on, because Steam reviews didn't exist before late 2013.
No re-releases of nineties classics. Those already had their moment. And one game per studio, or a single developer would take three spots.
Then I sorted by one number: how many times short of its expected reviews each game landed.
Fifteen thousand games cleared the bar to be judged. Ten of them got robbed the worst. Let's count down.
Number ten. Quell. A puzzle game you can get for about four dollars. Ninety-seven percent positive.
My model expected around three thousand two hundred reviews. It has four hundred and thirty-eight.
Want to know why? Look at the calendar. Quell came out on May 14th, 2015.
Four days later, The Witcher 3 launched. I don't think I'd have noticed a quiet puzzle game that week either.
Number nine. Bullet Heaven 2. A bullet-hell shooter where you dodge hundreds of bullets a second.
Ninety-eight percent positive. That's the highest rating in the whole top ten. Seven point six times short.
It came out on December 7th, 2015. Rainbow Six Siege had launched six days before.
Siege now has over a million reviews. Bullet Heaven 2 has four hundred and ninety-three.
Number eight. Paint it Back. You solve logic puzzles to restore pixel art.
It's the kind of game people sink a whole weekend into. Five hundred and forty-two reviews. The model wanted more than four thousand.
Number seven. Copy Kitty. You copy enemy powers and combine up to three of them into one super-weapon.
Ninety-seven percent positive, eight times short of where it should be. This one's on sale for under four dollars right now, by the way.
Number six. Marvin's Mittens. No enemies, no danger. You just explore.
Two hundred and five reviews against an expected seventeen hundred.
And five days after it launched, Geometry Dash came out. That game has four hundred and thirty thousand reviews now.
Okay, quick detour, because I expected a different game to be here.
Tadpole Treble scored ninety on Metacritic. That's higher than anything else on this list.
It only has two hundred and eighty reviews. But my model judges games by what players thought, not critics, and it's six point three times short.
Underrated, for sure. Just not top ten. The next five are even worse off.
Number five. Escape Goat 2. A puzzle platformer where you team up with a mouse to get out of a dungeon.
The first Escape Goat would have made this list too. It got cut because it came out before Steam reviews existed.
Four hundred and forty-one reviews. Ten point four times short.
Number four is a visual novel. Supipara, Chapter One. Ninety-eight percent positive from two hundred and fifty-five reviews.
Here's what's strange about it. A third of its English reviews showed up in just the last two years. People are still finding it, ten years later.
Number three. Blackwell Epiphany, the final game in the Blackwell series from Wadjet Eye.
Nine hundred and thirty-four reviews sounds like a lot until you see the expectation. Over ten thousand. That's eleven times short.
Number two surprised me. It's a solitaire game.
SHENZHEN SOLITAIRE started as a mini-game inside Zachtronics' SHENZHEN I/O, then got released on its own for three dollars.
Ninety-seven percent positive. The model expected twenty-five hundred reviews. It has two hundred and eight. Twelve times short.
Which brings us back to the red dot from the start.
Number one is twenty-one point eight times short of what my model expected. Nobody else on the list comes close.
For a game this well liked, from 2015, the typical count is about six thousand six hundred reviews. It has three hundred and two.
It's Gravity Ghost, by Ivy Games. You run, jump, and glide around tiny planets using gravity, rescuing survivors across a shattered galaxy.
Ninety-six percent positive. Seventy-five on Metacritic.
And here's the day it launched. January 26th, 2015.
The same day as Dying Light. Dying Light has four hundred and fifty-seven thousand reviews. Gravity Ghost has three hundred and two.
This is every month of Gravity Ghost's life on Steam. A small spike at launch, then a trickle that never fully stopped.
You can't really blame anyone. That week, everybody was fighting zombies.
So that's my list. I'm sure your favourite hidden gem isn't on it, so tell me which game the model missed.
Next time I'm flipping the model around: the most overrated game on Steam. That one's going to start some fights.
